name: Renee McGregor
who: Registered Dietitian (HCPC), clinical and performance nutrition specialist; dietitian for GB Olympic (2012), Paralympic (2016) and Commonwealth Games (2018) teams.
why: Leading global voice on RED-S and the female athlete; bestselling author (Training Food, Fast Fuel, Orthorexia) bridging endurance performance and eating-disorder care.
takeaway: Fuel your training adequately rather than under-eating, especially in endurance or aesthetic-focused sport.

name: Marie Spano
who: MS, RD, CSCS, CSSD; sports dietitian for the Washington Nationals and Atlanta Hawks, previously the Atlanta Braves (2017-2022, World Series champions 2021) and Atlanta Falcons.
why: One of the most tenured active pro-team dietitians in the US, spanning MLB, NBA and NFL; lead author of the textbook Nutrition for Sport, Exercise and Health.
takeaway: Treat sport-specific fueling as a coached skill tailored to your sport, not a generic diet plan.

name: Nancy Clark
who: MS, RD, CSSD; private sports-nutrition practice near Boston since the 1980s.
why: Author of Nancy Clark's Sports Nutrition Guidebook, one of the field's most widely used reference texts across multiple editions; trained a generation of sports RDs.
reach: Niche/legacy reach, no major social platform (not verified live)
takeaway: Match your everyday eating pattern to your training schedule using a proven sports-nutrition reference.

name: Louise Burke
who: PhD, APD; Professor and Chair in Sports Nutrition, Mary MacKillop Institute, Australian Catholic University; 30 years as Head of Sports Nutrition / Chief of Nutrition Strategy at the Australian Institute of Sport.
why: Australian Olympic team dietitian across five Games (1996-2012); 350+ peer-reviewed papers, editor of the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism; awarded the Order of Australia for her contribution to sports nutrition.
reach: Academic/professional reach, not a personal-brand social presence (verified via search 2026-08)
takeaway: Periodize your fueling like your training — carbs are a training variable, not a moral one.

name: Asker Jeukendrup
who: PhD; Director of Mysportscience Ltd, an independent sports-science and nutrition consultancy; 30 years as researcher, educator and practitioner, including a period leading Gatorade Sports Science Institute research.
why: His carbohydrate-oxidation and multiple-transportable-carbohydrate research reshaped modern endurance fueling protocols now standard across pro cycling and running.
reach: Newsletter/podcast audience, IG approx. mid-tens of thousands (verified business/role via site fetch 2026-08, reach not verified)
takeaway: Mix multiple carbohydrate sources during long efforts to raise how much fuel your gut absorbs.

name: Trent Stellingwerff
who: PhD; sport physiologist/nutrition lead at the Canadian Sport Institute Pacific, supporting Team Canada Olympic and world-championship athletes.
why: Applied "mission nutrition" performance frameworks used across Canadian high-performance sport; active researcher-practitioner bridging lab science and Games-time fueling.
takeaway: Plan fueling around the specific demands of competition day, not just your daily training.

name: James Collins
who: SENr-registered performance nutritionist; founder of Performance Nutrition, longtime nutrition consultant to Arsenal FC and England Rugby.
why: One of the most established practitioner names in elite UK football and rugby nutrition, with a multi-decade consultancy client list of pro clubs and national teams.
reach: Primarily B2B/club-facing, limited public social presence (not verified live)
takeaway: Coordinate what you eat with your training load, as part of a team performance plan.

name: Graeme Close
who: PhD; Professor of Human Physiology, Liverpool John Moores University; nutrition consultant to England Rugby and the PGA European Tour.
why: Bridges academic research on vitamin D, protein and player welfare with hands-on consultancy for elite rugby and golf, frequently cited in UK sports-science media.
reach: Academic/media reach, not a personal social brand (not verified live)
takeaway: Treat vitamin D and protein status as routine athlete care, not an afterthought.

name: Meghann Featherstun
who: RD, CSSD, known as "The Marathon Nutritionist"; runs a private practice and online coaching for runners at Featherstun Nutrition.
why: Built one of the largest audiences in run-specific fueling education, translating clinical sports-nutrition guidance into practical marathon and half-marathon fueling content.
reach: IG approx. 400-600K (handle confirmed live 2026-08, follower count not verified)
takeaway: Practice your race-day fueling plan in training long before the actual marathon or half.

name: Kylee Van Horn
who: RD specializing in trail and ultrarunning nutrition; works one-on-one with professional trail and ultra athletes.
why: One of the few dietitians with a dedicated ultra-endurance/trail-running client base, filling a gap most sports-nutrition figures don't cover.
takeaway: Get fueling advice specific to your event distance and terrain — ultra-endurance needs differ from shorter races.

name: Stephanie Howe
who: PhD in Nutrition and Exercise Physiology, RD; former elite ultrarunner (Western States 100 champion) now consulting with endurance athletes.
why: Rare combination of doctoral research training, RD credential and elite athletic pedigree, giving her fueling guidance unusual credibility in the ultra-endurance space.
takeaway: Treat fueling as trainable — practice eating and drinking under effort the way you practice running.

name: Alex Larson
who: RD, CSSD; founder of Fuel2Run, a practice coaching endurance runners on fueling and RED-S prevention.
why: Consistent, practical endurance-runner-focused education and coaching, filling the day-to-day fueling advice gap for recreational-to-competitive runners.
takeaway: Get individualized fueling coaching as a runner to avoid under-fueling and RED-S risk.

name: Jose Antonio
who: PhD; co-founder and CEO of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), professor at Nova Southeastern University.
why: Runs the field's leading professional/research society and its position stands on protein and supplementation, shaping how sports-nutrition guidelines are written and cited worldwide.
takeaway: Base supplement and protein choices on sports-nutrition society position stands, not marketing.

name: Susan Kleiner
who: PhD, RD, FACN, CNS; consults with professional and Olympic athletes and strength/physique competitors.
why: Author of Power Eating, a foundational strength-and-physique sports-nutrition text now in multiple editions, with decades of continuous elite-athlete consulting.
takeaway: Structure your protein intake and timing around training sessions if your goal is strength or physique.

name: Bob Seebohar
who: MS, RD, CSSD, CSCS; sports dietitian for USA Triathlon across multiple Olympic cycles, founder of Fuel4mance.
why: Longtime Olympic-team practitioner known for periodized/metabolic-efficiency fueling approaches adopted across endurance coaching.
takeaway: Periodize your carbohydrate intake across the season, not just race day, to build flexibility.

name: Dan Benardot
who: PhD, RD; professor emeritus, Georgia State University; nutrition consultant to US Olympic gymnastics and figure-skating programs.
why: Academic authority on energy availability and micro-periodized eating for aesthetic/weight-sensitive sports, author of the textbook Advanced Sports Nutrition.
reach: Academic reach, no notable social platform (not verified live)
takeaway: Spread your energy intake evenly across the day rather than swinging between under- and over-eating.

name: Alan McCubbin
who: PhD; senior lecturer at Monash University and Sports Dietitians Australia member, consulting with elite triathletes and endurance athletes.
why: Active gut-training and carbohydrate-fueling researcher whose work informs current endurance-nutrition practice guidelines in Australia and beyond.
takeaway: Train your gut to tolerate more carbohydrate during exercise gradually, the same way you train muscle.

name: Amy Goodson
who: MS, RD, CSSD; sports dietitian for the Dallas Cowboys and multiple pro and college athletic programs.
why: One of the more visible NFL team dietitians in US sports media, regularly quoted on pro-athlete fueling and recovery nutrition.
takeaway: Prioritize a recovery meal or snack soon after hard training, as pro-team athletes are coached to.

name: Chris Rosenbloom
who: PhD, RDN, CSSD; professor emerita, Georgia State University; nutrition consultant to the Atlanta Ballet and collegiate athletes.
why: Widely cited sports-nutrition textbook co-author and educator who helped formalize sports RD training programs in the US.
reach: Academic reach, no notable social platform (not verified live)
takeaway: Learn the fundamentals of sports fueling from a textbook-level source before trusting quick tips.
